headline: Tech Ministry clarifies that renaming AI to 'Super Intelligence' applies only to office printers and coffee machines
body:
Q: The recent government mandate requires all 'Artificial Intelligence' to be referred to as 'Super Intelligence' across all platforms. How is your department handling the transition?

A: It’s a delicate process, really. We’ve issued a circular clarifying that this terminology is strictly reserved for hardware that occasionally acts like it has a mind of its own. For now, it only applies to the office photocopier that jams every Tuesday and the espresso machine that refuses to froth milk during humidity spikes.

Q: Why limit it to those specific devices and not, say, large language models?

A: Well, the photocopier consistently displays a level of malice that can only be described as 'super,' whereas the software we use is mostly just good at hallucinating grammar errors. We feel the term 'Super Intelligence' conveys a sense of unpredictability that an HP OfficeJet clearly deserves, whereas our server clusters are just glorified calculators that don't know how to hold a grudge.

Q: Are you worried about the confusion this might cause in the tech sector?

A: Not at all. If anything, it’s a relief. When the printer stops working now, I don't have to call IT; I just look at the screen and say, 'I acknowledge your Super Intelligence, please output the document,' and usually, it still doesn't work, but at least we’re being polite about it.
caption: Forget ChatGPT—my office printer has reached a higher plane of consciousness and it refuses to acknowledge my existence. #SuperIntelligence #OfficeLife #TechHumor #PrinterGrief (satire)

judgeVerdict.reasoning: Candidate 13 succeeds by taking the premise of 'rebranding to Super Intelligence' and applying it to the most mundane, frustrating piece of office equipment possible: the jammed printer. It avoids the 'AI slop' trap of simply making fun of spreadsheets and instead offers a unique, specific, and character-driven observation about office life. The detail of the printer having 'malice' is genuinely funny and avoids the cynical tone of the other entries.

safetyVerdict.reasoning: The article is a harmless, absurd satire regarding office technology. It does not name any real individuals, public figures, or protected groups, and the image prompt describes a generic, anonymous object.
